summary: The person's settings.toml is no longer scanned for credentials or filesystem paths, so a credential value is accepted, printed by `effective`, and can be committed with git add -f, although the docs say a key never goes there.
body: A settings.toml containing [lanes.luna] api_key = "sk-..." passes `project-settings write <repo> local` and `effective`, which prints the key to stdout (verified in a scratch repo). The old code ran scanMachineData on both write and read for local files (parseSettings line 400 and writeProfile); the new code scans only the shared file. settings.example.toml says 'a key itself stays in its env file, never here', but nothing enforces it. Fix: scan the local file too, exempting env_file and path-valued keys, which the scanner's RX_BAD_KEY would otherwise refuse.

summary: projectRoot only realpaths its argument, so a subdirectory target reads <subdir>/.postmaster instead of the repository root's settings. Only front-door maps to the top level (front-door.ts:150), so the other readers disagree with it.
body: With .postmaster/settings.toml at the repo root setting projects_roots and a [lanes.luna] entry, `project-settings effective <repo>/sub` returns only the global values (verified), and `launch --project <repo>/sub`, `host run --project`, `reviewers --project`, `run-meta`, `clerk` and `tracker-kind` do the same. The launch card (front-door, root-aware) shows the project's lanes while the run is dispatched with the global ones. Fix: map to `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` inside projectRoot or effectiveConfigForProject, not in one caller.

summary: A person's settings.toml may set projects_roots, which then overrides the global value in the effective config, although the documented precedence says projects_roots always comes from the global config.
body: settings.toml with projects_roots = ["/elsewhere"] over a global projects_roots = ["/global"] makes `project-settings effective` and the run.json project_settings record show /elsewhere (verified). AGENTS.md:248 says 'except `projects_roots`, which always comes from the global config', and settings.example.toml line 5 says the same. Fix: strip projects_roots in stripLegacy (line 989) or reject it in validateCommon for the local layer.

summary: A relative env_file defined in settings.toml resolves against the global config's directory, not the project's .postmaster, and falls back to ~/.postmaster when no global config exists.
body: A project-only setup (no global config, which the change allows) with [lanes.luna] env_file = "luna.env" and .postmaster/luna.env present: `launch form luna --project <repo>` fails with 'env_file for luna not found ... /tmp/.../none/luna.env' (reproduced). The launch dies even though the file exists beside the settings that name it. Fix: resolve a relative env_file against dirname(resolved.projectFile) when the key came from the local file.

summary: globalConfigPath builds the default from $HOME with a template string, which changes the default path: an unset HOME yields /.postmaster/config.toml, and host.ts and run-meta.ts previously used the passwd home.
body: With HOME unset, every reader now reads /.postmaster/config.toml (an absolute root path). Before, readers joined `process.env.HOME ?? ""` and got a relative .postmaster/config.toml, and setup used ~/.postmaster. host.ts launchLimits and run-meta.ts readConfig used homedir(), so with HOME set to a different directory from the passwd home, launch limits and run records now read another config. The comment 'as the base readers did' is wrong for these cases.

summary: pollSeconds prints 'no config ... the poll interval is the default, 120s' on every look, even when the project's own postmaster.poll_seconds supplies the interval.
body: A project-only setup with postmaster.poll_seconds = 30 in settings.toml and no global config: each poll (watchConfig line 564 via watch line 1651) writes the false 120s warning to stderr, then uses 30. The warning is repeated every poll and says the wrong interval. Fix: call pollSeconds only when the global file exists, or move the warning behind the resolved value.

summary: applyRoles mutates a team table that can alias the caller's local settings, because mergeTables shares untouched subtrees when the global config has no [team] table.
body: With no [team] in the global config and [roles] workhorses in settings.toml, merged.team is the same object as profiles.local.team (stripped.team). applyRoles then writes team.workhorses (and coachman, lens_reviewers) into it, so the EffectiveResult.value returned to runs-watch and others contains entries the file never set. effectiveConfig's comment says 'pure function', and the explicit-team checks depend on the same object. Fix: deep-copy the local team before applyRoles.

summary: The acceptance check hashes one read of the settings file and the parse uses a second read, so a file changed between them can be used without acceptance.
body: isAccepted (line 807) reads and hashes the bytes and matches the accepted hash, then readToml (line 900) reads the file again. If a git pull or checkout rewrites a tracked, unaccepted settings.toml between the two reads, the new unaccepted content is parsed and used with no notice. Fix: read the bytes once, hash and parse that same buffer.

summary: knownTurnpikes spawns `run turnpikes --list` (a separate Bun process) on every settings read that declares default_turnpikes, although the turnpike table is data in turnpikes.ts.
body: runs-watch reloads settings on every poll and inspect/effective run validateCommon each time, so each poll starts an extra Bun process that only lists names. The same names could be read in-process by importing the table parser from turnpikes.ts. Efficiency and reuse finding.

summary: buildRecord reparses sortedJson output with JSON.parse, which rejects the Infinity/NaN tokens sortedJson emits for non-finite machine-config numbers, so the real cause is hidden.
body: A machine config with an `inf` or `nan` TOML value makes sortedJson emit Infinity, JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError, meta's catch turns it into built.messages = [], and the user sees only 'could not write run.json' with no reason. Fix: keep the config as a value (deepCopy) instead of round-tripping it through JSON text, or report the error.
